log b1

Deliverables: 14-01-27 (midnight)


 

Previous Block: A
Previous Block’s Feedback:
-> to be added when the Block A feedback is returned
What I Learned Last Block:
-> Test a doubtful idea early and small, before building on it. The extra week on embedding maps gave me a clear reason for dropping them.
-> Real examples show a gap far better than abstract description. Table 1 did more work than any paragraph I wrote about it.
-> Changing the order of an argument also changes which words need defining first.
-> Diagrams are a test of understanding: a wrong arrow is easier to spot than a vague sentence.
What I Need To Work On Now:
-> Turn the methodology note into Chapter 3. That note was written before my literature review was finished, so every part of it needs checking against the review before it goes in.
-> Decide how players talk (typed, voice or both) before any code depends on it.
-> Start the game build small: a paper prototype for the rules, and the networking layer first, so it is out of the way early.
-> Keep the risk assessment as a living document, and go through it with my supervisors at the start of the block.

Current Block: B
What I Want To Achieve This Block (& How?):
-> Write the methodology, and the first findings
> Chapter 3: Methodology (with a hypothesis and a full ethics review)
> Chapter 4: Data & Results (early findings from the pilots)
Plan the chapter before writing it, section by section, like the Literature Review Plan in Block A. Base the method on existing commons experiments and asymmetric game studies rather than inventing it from scratch. Talk the ethics review over with my first reader. Keep regular meetings with my first & second reader, and keep checking the plan against the ILOs.
-> Build the game, and prove it gives me usable data
> A networked game that logs every proposal, action and report
> Pilots in stages: paper prototype -> scripted agents -> human groups
Lock the platform and the talk mode by the end of week 2. Build the networking and logging first, and test the rules on paper alongside the code. Run every pilot through the full data pipeline, from game log to the final measures, so I find the gaps before Block C and not during it.
-> Get feedback from outside Buas
> From people who run or design commons games
Show the methodology to colleagues from the Ecopoly / CETIP side, and reach out to researchers working on commons experiments or co-operative game design. Write down what each person said, and what I changed (or didn't change) because of it.
-> Publish reusable artefacts
> Game, logging and analysis code
Put the code on GitHub with documentation, like MapTheGap, so other researchers can run or adapt the same experiment. No participant data goes public.
-> Keep teaching and community work going
> DAE teaching, guilds and workshops
Keep logging everything in Community Contributions, with evidence.
-> Keep reading, keep balance
> Keep up regular reading, inside and outside of my research
> Keep job work and study work apart
Thursdays stay for Buas. Keep the priority list, so I know what can be paused in a busy week. The winter break is a spare week for pilots if they run over, but otherwise it is real rest.

20_publish/learning-logs/learning-log---.title: Learning Log - Block Outro - A
20_publish/learning-logs/learning-log---.content:
log


                  
                  Important Dates 
                  
                

Presentations: 28-10-26 & 29-10-26
Deliverables: 30-10-26 (midnight)


 

Current Block: A
My Plan For This Block Was:
-> Begin writing the thesis: a first introduction and the literature review.
-> Complete my “teaching” ILO with the Blender/Arduino classes at DAE.
-> Get back into regular reading, and understand more technical approaches to ML (especially ML and maps).
-> Balance my job research with my studies.
How I Performed This Block:
-> The introduction and literature review are both written, submitted, and presented. The research question took 14 iterations to get there.
-> The teaching ILO is under way: the DAE class was planned & executed and the Blender lessons recorded.
-> The ML goal changed shape. I tested the TESSERA embedding maps, then dropped them in week 5 as interesting-but-too-complex. Most of my reading moved from books to papers and commercial game rulebooks.
-> Job and study balance relied on keeping set days just for Buas. The block plan shifted almost every week, but each change is logged as internal or external, so I can see where the time went.

State of the Thesis:
-> Title: Who Knows, Who Acts? Separating knowledge from power in an asymmetric commons game.
-> Written: Introduction (Ch. 1) and Literature Review (Ch. 2, six sections, 10 figures and a table comparing games against the gap). The order is games first, governance second.
-> Still to write: Abstract, Acknowledgements, and Chapters 3-6. Chapter 3 already exists as a working methodology note (two setups played by every group, 12 groups of 4, ~90 minute sessions), but none of it is in the thesis yet.
-> Open decisions: whether players talk by typing, voice, or both. Which platform to build the game on.

Significant Achievements This Block:
-> A final research question that works for both fields, with every iteration published so the supervisors can follow how it changed.
-> MapTheGap, my own tool for mapping citation links in Zotero, which I now cite as a source in the thesis.
-> Flipping the narrative to games -> governance across the presentation, introduction and literature review in one week, without losing the argument.
What Challenged Me This Block:
-> Letting go of the embedding maps. Spending an extra week to prove they were the wrong route felt slow, but it gave me a clear argument for not using them.
-> Citing commercial games. There are no page numbers and a lot of online claims cannot be checked, so I only use rulebooks and publisher pages.
-> Making a late structural change (the flip) close to the deadline, during the autumn holiday.
What Did I Learn This Block:
-> Test a doubtful idea early and small, before building on it (thanks to my first reader for suggesting this!).
-> Real examples show a gap far better than abstract description. Table 1 does more work than any paragraph I wrote about it.
-> Changing the order of an argument also changes which words need defining first (“levers” became “the power to act”).
-> Diagrams are a test of understanding: a wrong arrow is easier to spot than a vague sentence.

Self-Assessment Grade: ~
I highly dislike doing this sort of self-assessment grading, and I find it less useful for my personal development. Therefore my answer is:
“A grade high enough that you empathise with my sense of self-worth, but low enough that you don’t feel I’m being overconfident in the first block of this Master’s thesis workload.”
I can justify my work below, but I prefer that a grade is something externally validated.
Why I Feel This Is Justified:
-> Both Block A deliverables (introduction and literature review) were submitted on time, with the presentation tested twice beforehand.
-> Every big decision (the pivot, the 14 question iterations, the flip) is logged with its reasoning in the weekly logs and published notes.
-> The literature review brings both fields together with equal weight, which is the core of the thesis.
How I Plan To Improve Next Block:
-> Turn the methodology note into Chapter 3, and decide on the talk mode before any piloting.
-> Start the game build early with a paper prototype (Tabletop Simulator) before writing game-design code. While pilot-simulating, start with the networked layer of the game, so it is out the way quickly.
-> Keep the risk assessment as a living document, and review it with my supervisors at the start of the block.

Amended Weekly Plan:

Introduction & Admin

 Learning Log template

 Zotero setup
 Notes <-> Citations workflow setup


Research Question Sketches

 Explore Buas Metasearch Library
 Create weekly plan (keeping in mind ILO’s)

 Initial risk assessment half-completed; could not attend the voluntary lecture on Risk-Assessment, and therefore need to re-watch it online to make my own risk assessmnent fully scoped.

Literature Reading & Self-Assessing

 Read through the major Foundational & Contrarian viewpoints across the research field(s). Abstract, Intro & Conclusion.
 Evaluate the self-made research graph. Assess where the research gaps are, and which papers are ‘closest’ to that gap.
 From the lecture ‘research approaches’ this week, give an outline of the possible research methods (first draft) that could be useful to consider
 For the Foundational & Contrarian papers (and those closest to my research topic) evaluate the ethics & quality of those sources


Begin Literature Review

 Check my literature review outline with existing papers, and ask First Reader for advice


Begin Introduction

Finalise Introduction & Literature Review, start Presentation

Finalise Presentation

 Practice presentation on peers & first supervisor
 Manage speaking time
 Assess the need of explaining definitions during presentation
 Balance sociological (Commons) vs technical (Tessera) verbal explanations
 Simplify presentation visuals; make it pretty!
 Do a final sweep of Learning Logs and important notes, for supervisors to view


Deadline & Presentations

^ note: record internal vs external influence factors.

Progress:
-> Created a flexible & easily maintainable tagging system for my Zotero sources database.
-> Figured out the Zotero API, so that I can batch-tag and batch process PDFs where necessary.
-> Asked Claude to make a simple visual graph of the sources publication timeline, citation interlinking, and tag linking.
-> Made a further graph that uses force-lines to visualise research gaps (and/or lack of source collection) between database sources. This way Claude is only used to create the visual; the tags and citation information does the rest of the work.
-> These graphs can then be used as a ‘literature process report’ across this semester, by simply exporting the graph at any point in time.
Research Source Graphs:

^ First research paper pass. Includes Foundational papers like Osrtom’s ‘Governing The Commons’, as well as her lectures on ‘Collective Action’. The right-side blob are all to do with Machine-Learning maps. No research connects the two subjects yet.

^ Second research paper pass. Includes more of Ostrom’s work across 1970-2009, as well as more recent additional papers that directly cite many of her works (such as ‘Institutional navigation for polycentric sustainability governance’). Also included in this pass are further ML papers and several research projects I have personal connection to. These can be seen as the grey dots floating inbetween the two separate research areas.

^ Third research paper pass. On this one I focused on papers directly relating to Ostrom’s work; especially more recent papers that actually take her work out of theory and into real practice. This revealed some Contrarian sources; especially around how the Commons theories treat power dynamics, and the lack of long-term behavioural studies on Commons-in-practice (e.g. ‘The black box of power in polycentric environmental governance’). One especially useful connectuve paper popped-up; ‘Smart Earth: A meta-review and implications for environmental governance’ - which will likely be useful in bridging the gap between the social and technical themes in my project.
Reflection:
-> I think the solution I found for Claude to make graphs, while I provide the citation information and tags, is a neat empirical solution to evaluating ‘research gaps’.
-> Stating the above; I do have to take my research visualisation with a pinch of salt, as the information/pattern output is only as good as the tags I provide.
-> My research is heavily leaning into the socio-economic theory; as research papers are much easier to find for that area. The theory is older, there is an active discussion since the 1960’s about the ‘Commons’ topic, and every paper tends to cite each other (making it very easy to evaluate argument patterns across multiple papers). However the more technical ‘Machine-Learning’ side is newer; which means fewer papers, fewer cross-citations (multiple papers coming out simultaneously don’t tend to cite each other), and similar problem ‘themes’ are often are solved with solutions where the technical stack is different.
Action Points
-> Start exporting my ‘research graphs’ and placing them in the learning logs dedicated section.
-> Look further out than research papers (blogs, github, etc) for information about Machine Learning, Embedding model application, and using ML in maps.

Risks & Mitigations:
-> risk There may be no discernable links between the map-machine-learning and the socio-economic theory of the Commons. mitigation If this ends up being the case, then use the literature review to explain this gap and why it makes my research particularly poignant.
-> risk As my work becomes more and more socio-economic focused, it is clearer that the eventual methodology will require qualitative data with groups of people. mitigation Use BUAS & DAE students for this, and plan well in advance. Note in the methodology (& presentations) that this was the approach due to time constraints, and show the intended ‘target audience’ if I had unlimited time and money.
^ note: record both risk factors and their related  mitigation plan.

Extra ILO’s:

^ Planning my Introduction to 3D class. For Design Academy Eindhoven 4th year students, this is a 6-day class that goes through 3D concepts, introduction to networked systems, microcontrollers into 3D editors, and environment building in Blender.

Progress:
-> Block A is submitted and presented!
-> This week was for planning. I re-read my introduction and literature review, the ILOs, the Block B section of the project brief, and all my Block A logs, and turned them into the plan above.
-> The brief asks for two chapters this block, not one: the methodology, and a short “test run” chapter that reports the pilot data without interpreting it. It also asks for a hypothesis. Both are now in the plan.
Reflection:
-> My methodology note is much bigger than one block. It has a twelve-month build schedule, an exact optimiser, a board generator and a pre-registration, and it was written before my literature review settled (it still says “typed only”, for example). I am treating it as a pile of ideas under review, not as the plan.
-> My week numbering does not match the Buas calendar. My weeks run Thursday to Thursday, so week 7 falls before Christmas and only week 8 comes after the break. Worth keeping in mind when lecture weeks and my weeks don’t line up.
-> The Block A plan changed almost every week. I expect the same here, especially once the pilots start, so I will keep logging every change as internal or external.
Action Points
-> Send this plan and the Block B risk review to my first reader, and agree meeting dates for the block.
-> Start the data minimum requirements, and collect experiment techniques from papers.

Risks & Mitigations:
-> risk My methodology note is too big for the time I have, and it was designed before the literature review was finished. mitigation Review it against the literature review in week 2, keep only what the research question needs, and use the cut list already in the note if I need to go further.
-> risk The game build runs late and eats into the pilot week. mitigation Networking and logging come first, in week 3. The paper prototype tests the rules while the code is being written, and the scripted agents test the pipeline before any people play. The winter break is spare time for one more pilot.
-> risk Finding pilot players in December is hard, with exams and holidays coming up. mitigation Start recruiting in weeks 4-5, fix dates early, and keep a backup group.
-> risk Two chapters and the presentation all land around the holiday, when my supervisors are harder to reach. mitigation Send the methodology draft at the end of week 6. Set up the early findings chapter so it fills in from the analysis script, and reuse my Block A diagrams in the presentation.
-> note The full Block B risk review, with the top risks for this block, is in Risk Assessment WIP.
^ note: record both risk factors and their related  mitigation plan.
